result.title: Complete the Alpine plants guide editorial review
result.summary: Clarifies how to use the safety labels, strengthens the exposure response steps, and preserves every plant classification and the visible editorial-review draft status without suggesting veterinary or botanical approval.

changes.before: Most plant encounters are harmless, but a few species can make a dog seriously ill if chewed or swallowed. Check ordinary proximity, what to prevent, and what to do after suspected ingestion.
changes.after: Some Alpine plants can make a dog seriously ill if chewed or swallowed. Use this guide to check which encounters need caution, prevent ingestion and respond promptly to a suspected exposure.
changes.reason: Removes a broad reassurance and states the guide’s practical purpose more clearly without changing any plant classification.

changes.before: Move your dog away and prevent more exposure. Call the nearest veterinarian or emergency clinic. For a red-status plant, call immediately and do not wait for symptoms.
changes.after: Move your dog away and prevent further exposure. Call a veterinarian or emergency clinic promptly, even if your dog has no symptoms yet. If the plant has red status, say so when you call and treat the situation as urgent.
changes.reason: Makes the immediate action clearer and avoids suggesting that an absence of symptoms rules out poisoning.

changes.before:
Trail-safe

Safe to walk near or sniff under normal conditions. It never means edible.
changes.after:
Trail-safe

Ordinary proximity or sniffing is not identified as a concern in this guide. The label never means edible.
changes.reason: Preserves the Trail-safe classification while defining its limited scope more precisely.

changes.before: All 13 records still require veterinarian and regional botanist sign-off. Until then, the page remains visibly labelled as an editorial-review draft. No unverified plant photographs are shown.
changes.after: All 13 records are part of this editorial-review draft and are not presented as approved by a veterinarian or regional botanist. The page remains visibly labelled as a draft, and no unverified plant photographs are shown.
changes.reason: Preserves the visible draft status while removing the implication that veterinary or botanical sign-off is expected or has occurred.

sources.supports: Supports contacting a veterinarian promptly after suspected poisoning and not inducing vomiting unless specifically directed.
